chunks: We said: This is the speech of one who thinks that it is obligatory upon us to empower him when he appears, and that this is not obligatory upon us in every condition,

but we accepted the example he mentioned, because if Allah, the Exalted, had made drawing water obligatory upon us at that moment, it would have been necessary that the rope be present at that moment, because through it the excuse is eliminated,
however, if He says: 'When you approach the well, I will create for you the rope,' then he is only obligated to approach, not to draw water,
so the ability to approach is sufficient in this condition, because he is not yet obligated to draw water from it,
so when he approaches the well, he then becomes obligated to draw water, and at that point it becomes necessary that the rope be created for him,
an analogous instance to this is that if it were not obligatory upon us in every condition to obey the Imam and empower him, then his existence would not be necessary at that time,

but since his obedience is obligatory at the present moment, and we do not know his condition or a waiting time, it becomes necessary that he be present to eliminate the excuse in the obligation, and this is fitting.
ai.seo_question: How does the analogy of the well and rope explain the necessity of the Imam's presence?
ai.summary: Al-Tusi employs the analogy of drawing water to resolve the logical tension between the perpetual obligation of obedience (ta'ah) and the conditional necessity of the Imam's physical presence (wujud). He argues that just as the rope is created only when one approaches the well—triggering the specific act of drawing water—the Imam's existence is required only when the condition for obedience is active, thereby refuting the view that his presence must be constant regardless of context. This reasoning underscores the Shia principle that the Imam's authority is functional and tied to the realization of divine commands.
